phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar [z] plus palatalized m [mʲ] and a diphthong [ej] — 'zm-YAY', the hissing onset of the serpent-word zmei.
Unstressed [ɡɐ] — the back of the name, the mountain lying low before the storm.
Stressed [ˈrɨnɨtɕ] with the rolled r and soft final [tɕ] — 'RY-nich', the syllable where the fire lands.

pronunciation.approximation: zm-YAY guh-RY-nich — stress on 'ry'; the final -nych is a soft, hissing 'nich', not 'nik'.

kin.label: Indo-Iranian
kin.form: Vedic ahí and Avestan aži, 'serpent' — cognates of zmei within Indo-European; the Avestan dragon Aži Dahāka is the same word's most famous bearer

kin.label: Russian
kin.form: Gorynych, from gora, 'mountain' — 'the one of the mountain'; his three heads breathe fire from the Sorochinsky heights

pronunciation.note: Zmeygorynych is Tier 2: the name is plain ASCII, and its Russian form Змей Горыныч is Cyrillic, outside the Latin restoration system — the transliteration loses no distinctive feature the ASCII alphabet could keep. The placeholder earlier note claiming the ASCII form was 'a DNS compromise' missed that the lexicon assigns Tier 2 mechanically.

domains.title: Zmey Gorynych
domains.subtitle: Three-Headed Dragon
domains.lead: Zmey Gorynych is the fire-breathing, three-headed dragon of the Russian byliny — terror of the Sorochinsky mountains, abductor of princesses, and the nemesis of the hero Dobrynya Nikitich. His name joins zmei, the Slavic dragon, with Gorynych, 'of the mountain': the serpent made into geography.

cards.name: Fire from Three Heads
cards.desc: Each head spits flame; the bylina says his breath scorched the mountains black and burnt the hero's clothing to ash.

cards.name: The Sorochinsky Mountains
cards.desc: His lair beyond the serpent's river — the ridge Dobrynya's mother forbade her son ever to ride toward.

cards.name: Princess Zabava
cards.desc: Prince Vladimir's niece, carried off twice — the abduction that forced the hero to break his oath and finish the fight.

cards.name: The Slayer's Oath
cards.desc: Dobrynya swore on his sword to let the beaten dragon live; mercy once given became the dragon's second chance — and the hero's second battle.

symbols.name: Three fire-breathing heads
symbols.meaning: The bylina numbers them three, each mouth a furnace — appetite that multiplies faster than it can be cut down

symbols.name: The Sorochinsky mountains
symbols.meaning: The named lair of the bylina world — the untamed margin beyond the river where heroes are told not to ride

symbols.name: The wet women's hat (mokryi golvnik)
symbols.meaning: The soaked cap Dobrynya holds against the flame — soaked wool, not steel, defeats dragonfire

symbols.name: The burnt neck-stumps
symbols.meaning: A zmei's severed heads grow back unless the stumps are burned — victory must be made irreversible

symbols.name: The serpent's river
symbols.meaning: The boundary where Dobrynya's horse stumbled — the omen-line between the hero's world and the dragon's

mythology.lead: The crown of the Dobrynya cycle: how a hero's mercy gave the dragon a second life, and how the second battle was won by a wet hat, not a sword. The byliny are oral epic, recorded from living singers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

myths.title: Dobrynya Rides to the Mountains
myths.text: In the bylina of Dobrynya Nikitich and Zmey Gorynych, recorded by the nineteenth-century collectors of the Kireevsky circle, the hero's mother warns him never to ride to the Sorochinsky mountains, for the fire-breathing serpent holds them. The young hero rides anyway. From a dark cloud the dragon descends with three heads, and fire pours from each mouth. They fight for three days — Dobrynya's arrows spent, his clothing burnt, the earth scorched black around them. At last the dragon begs for mercy: let me go, brave Dobrynya, and I will never again carry off Christian people. The hero remembers his mother's teaching — she who spared the serpent brought grief upon herself — but he sheathes his sword and lets the dragon go. The bylina's first lesson is mercy; its second, still to come, is what mercy costs when it is spent on a dragon.

myths.title: The Second Battle and the Wet Hat
myths.text: The dragon keeps neither his word nor his fear. He seizes Zabava, niece of Prince Vladimir, and carries her to his mountain. Dobrynya rides after him, but at the serpent's river his horse stumbles and refuses the water — an omen he cannot ignore. The second battle is worse than the first: flame no shield can face. Dobrynya survives by his mother's counsel — he soaks his women's hat in the river and fights beneath the dripping hood, the wet wool hissing where the fire strikes it. When the dragon weakens, Dobrynya cuts off all three heads, then gathers the severed stumps and burns them, for a zmei's heads grow back if they are allowed to rejoin; finally he bathes in the dragon's blood and returns Zabava to her uncle's hall. The detail every singer kept is the wet hat: the weapon that wins the second battle is not steel but preparation — soaked wool against dragonfire, and the patience to finish what mercy left unfinished.

myths.title: The Tribute of Maidens
myths.text: Outside the bylina, in the fairy-tale corpus gathered by Afanas'ev in the nineteenth century, the three-headed zmei belongs to a darker economy. He descends on a town and names his price: maidens, nine at a time, year after year, and the townsfolk pay, because the alternative is fire. These are anonymous tales of the ATU 300 dragon-slayer type, and the dragon's hunger here is less personal than the bylina's — he is not anyone's nemesis, he is the thing the community feeds. A peasant's third son, the fool of the family, marks his arrows and climbs to the lair. In these tales the dragon-slayer is almost never the expected one: not the king's champion but the youngest brother, the one nobody fed to the serpent. The tribute myth turns the whole village into an accomplice, and the slayer into the one who finally refused to pay — the point being that dragons are affordable only until someone counts the cost.

myths.title: The Epic as Archive
myths.text: The bylina itself had to be saved as often as the princess. It survived in the mouths of peasant singers in the Russian north until the mid-eighteenth century, when the compiler Kirsha Danilov set down the earliest known collection of byliny, and again in the 1860s when P. V. Kireevsky's expeditions took the songs from living performers whose grandmothers had sung them. Folklorists from Veselovsky to Propp argued over the dragon's ancestry: a pagan storm-serpent, they proposed, overlaid with the Christian St George — the folk hero Dobrynya standing in for the saint, the dragon for the devil of the iconostasis. Propp, in his Russian Epic Studies, read the dragon fight as a seasonal spring rite pressed into epic form. Whatever the origin, the song outlived every theory about it. The epic is the only weapon in the cycle that never had to be reforged: as long as someone sings it, the dragon stays slain and alive at once.

lore.syncretism: Scholars read the bylina dragon through two overlays. The older stratum is pagan: the Slavic zmei descends from Proto-Slavic *zmьjь, kin to Vedic ahí and Avestan aži, the great serpents of Indo-Iranian myth, and some hear in Dobrynya's duel a faint memory of the storm god's war on the chthonic snake. The visible stratum is Christian: after the baptism of Rus the zmei absorbed the devil's portfolio — fire, the wilderness, the carrying-off of Christians — and folklorists showed how closely the duel tracks the iconography of St George and the Dragon, the saint's spring feast of Yuri's Day folded into the ritual year. In the Soviet century the dragon was nationalized into a fairy-tale villain, and Aleksandr Ptushko's 1956 film Ilya Muromets gave him his definitive pop-culture body, a towering three-headed puppet. In the internet age Gorynych became an ironic self-emblem of Russia: three heads, one fire, famously hard to kill. The layers never replaced one another; the dragon simply grew a new head each century and kept all the old ones.
lore.culturalLegacy: The byliny are still sung — by folk ensembles in the Russian north and by animators in Moscow — and Zmey Gorynych remains their star monster. His name is the Russian byword for any three-headed menace, from political caricature to sports mascots; 'Gorynych' alone summons the whole image of fire, mountains, and tribute. The 2006 animated feature Dobrynya Nikitich and Zmey Gorynych introduced him to children three generations removed from the last village singers, and Ptushko's 1956 dragon puppet is studied as a landmark of practical-effects cinema. In the global fantasy mainstream he is now the default Slavic dragon — three heads, mountain lair, maidens' tribute — read back into novels and games by writers who never heard a bylina performed. The song outlived the singers; the dragon, characteristically, outlived the song.
lore.extendedMeditation: Zmey Gorynych is the dragon you negotiate with. Three heads, three fires, one appetite — and the bylina's hard wisdom is that appetite does not retire when beaten; it waits, remembers, and tests the terms. Dobrynya's first mistake is the forgivable one: he believes the dragon's promise, because honor is how heroes think, and dragons do not. The second battle is the real education — fought under a wet hat, won with preparation, and sealed by burning the stumps so nothing grows back. The dragon in the mountains is the part of the world that cannot be argued with, only out-prepared. Every community has one: the river that floods, the fire that returns, the appetite that renames itself each season. The epic's counsel is unglamorous and permanent — soak your hat, watch the stumps, and never confuse a dragon's exhaustion with its surrender. Mercy is a virtue; verified mercy is a strategy.

lore.archaeology: No monument names Zmey Gorynych; the evidence is textual and pictorial rather than excavated. The dragon lives first in manuscripts — Kirsha Danilov's mid-eighteenth-century collection, the Kireevsky recordings of the 1860s, and the later Gil'ferding expedition collections from the Russian north. He lives second in the folk image: lubok woodcuts of the dragon fight sold at fairs from the seventeenth century onward, and the iconographic type of St George and the Dragon, which popular art quietly converted into Dobrynya's battle. Medieval Russian church sculpture and manuscript margins supply the serpent of Genesis and the dragon of the Apocalypse — the visual stock from which the bylina's Gorynych was assembled. The most vivid material witness is the most recent: the towering three-headed puppet built for Aleksandr Ptushko's film Ilya Muromets (1956), still the most-seen Gorynych ever made.
